prompt: `toylm info` ends with `parameters: 436 stored counts`. What are those 436 parameters?

choices.text: The counts the model learnt, which are the whole model
choices.why: Right. `toylm save` writes them to a file, and that file is the model.

choices.text: The settings you can pass to `toylm generate`, such as the temperature
choices.why: Those are sampling controls, chosen per request. They are not part of the model.

choices.text: The sentences of the corpus, kept so the model can find them again
choices.why: No sentence is stored. The file holds counts of which word followed which.

choices.text: The number of distinct words in its vocabulary
choices.why: The vocabulary is 72 words. The 436 are counts across three tables.

prompt: `model.json` holds `'coffee is': {'bitter': 1, 'cold': 2, 'hot': 16, 'ready': 3, 'strong': 5}`. You change `16` to `1` and run `toylm next "the coffee is"` from the edited file. What happens?
hint: The percentages come from these counts and from nothing else.

choices.text: Nothing, since the corpus still says the coffee is hot
choices.why: The corpus was only used to fill in the counts. Once the counts exist, they are the model.

choices.text: `hot` still leads, because the model remembers its training
choices.why: There is no memory outside the counts. The file is the whole model.

choices.text: The model refuses to load the file because the counts no longer match
choices.why: Nothing checks the counts against the corpus. It loads whatever numbers are there.

choices.text: `strong` leads, and `hot` drops to about 8%
choices.why: Right. The total becomes 12, so `strong` has 5 of 12 and `hot` 1 of 12. Change a parameter and the model changes.

prompt: What is a weight in a large language model?
hint: How does it get its value?

choices.text: A count of how often a word followed another
choices.why: That is `toylm`'s kind of parameter. A neural network's weights are learnt numbers, not counts.

choices.text: A sentence the model read in training, compressed so it can be retrieved
choices.why: The weights do not store sentences you could retrieve. What it read is spread across all of them.

choices.text: A number learnt in training, with no meaning of its own
choices.why: Right. No single one has a meaning you could read; the behaviour comes from all of them together.

choices.text: How much each word in your prompt matters
choices.why: That changes with every prompt. Weights are fixed once training is over.

prompt: How does training give the weights their values?
hint: What is checked after each prediction?

choices.text: Programmers set them by hand, one rule at a time
choices.why: Nobody sets billions of numbers by hand. They start random and are adjusted automatically.

choices.text: Each one is nudged towards making the real next token more likely
choices.why: Right. Repeated over enormous amounts of text, the nudges add up to grammar, facts and structure.

choices.text: They are copied from the counts of a trigram model of the same text
choices.why: No count table is involved. A network learns its own numbers from its errors.

choices.text: Each weight is assigned to one fact and filled in with it
choices.why: No weight holds one fact. Facts, as far as a model has them, are spread across many weights.

prompt: Which of these are true of a large model you are chatting with? Choose all that apply.
hint: Where does what it "remembers" in the chat come from?

choices.text: Its weights are the same at the end of the chat as at the start
choices.why: Yes. Using a model does not change its weights.

choices.text: What it recalls from earlier in the chat was sent to it again as input
choices.why: Yes. The earlier turns are part of the text it is given, lesson 4.

choices.text: Correcting it updates its weights, so tomorrow it will remember
choices.why: A correction lives in this conversation's text. The weights do not change because of it.

choices.text: You can search its weights for a sentence it read in training
choices.why: What it read is spread across all of its weights. There is nothing to search.

prompt: A model described as 70B has seventy ___ weights.
hint: B is a word, not a unit of memory.

prompt: Two models are both 7B. What can you conclude about them from that alone?
hint: What does the count decide exactly, and what does it not?

choices.text: They give the same answers, since they have the same parameters
choices.why: The same number of weights is not the same weights. Their values differ.

choices.text: They were trained on the same amount of text
choices.why: The count says nothing about how much text either one read.

choices.text: Both are worse than every 70B model at every task
choices.why: Size is not quality. A smaller model can do better on a given task.

choices.text: They need the same memory at the same width, and still differ a lot in quality
choices.why: Right. The count fixes the memory; training data and training time decide much of the quality.

prompt: An article says a model "has memorised the internet". What does this lesson say is wrong with the picture?
hint: Could you find a web page inside the weights?

choices.text: Models were never trained on web pages
choices.why: Much training text comes from the web. The point is what the weights are, not where the text came from.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong: the weights are the internet compressed, and can be decompressed
choices.why: There is no decompression that gives the pages back. The text left patterns in numbers, not a copy.

choices.text: Its weights are numbers shaped by the text, not a copy of it
choices.why: Right. That is why it writes text found nowhere in its training data, and why it gets facts it read wrong.

choices.text: It only memorised the parts that fit in its context window
choices.why: The context window is the text of one request, lesson 4. It has nothing to do with training.

prompt: How many gigabytes do the weights of a 13B model take at 16 bits?
hint: Parameters times bytes per parameter. Sixteen bits is two bytes.

prompt: How many gigabytes do the weights of a 70B model take at 4 bits?
A model's weights take 8 GB at 8 bits. How many gigabytes would they take at 32 bits?
hint: Count the bytes per weight at each width.

prompt: `quant.py` rounded four numbers to 4 bits. What happened to `0.0173`?
hint: Read the 4-bit line of the capture.

choices.text: It stayed exactly the same, as the largest of the four did
choices.why: The largest number sets the step and is always kept exactly. The smallest is the one most at risk.

choices.text: It became 0.0162, an error of about one thousandth
choices.why: That is the 8-bit result. At 4 bits the steps are far coarser.

choices.text: It grew to match the other weights
choices.why: Rounding moves a number to the nearest step; it does not pull small numbers up.

choices.text: It became 0
choices.why: Right. At 4 bits the step was larger than the number, so it rounded to zero and whatever it contributed is gone.

prompt: What does quantising a model from 16 bits to 4 bits trade?
hint: What is lost when a number is rounded?

choices.text: Speed for accuracy, since 4-bit models are always more accurate
choices.why: Rounding loses information. A 4-bit model is never more accurate than the same model at 16 bits.

choices.text: Weights for parameters
choices.why: Those are two names for the same numbers. Quantising keeps all of them and stores each one in fewer bits.

choices.text: The number of weights, which falls from seven billion to under two
choices.why: The count is unchanged. Each weight takes fewer bits.

choices.text: Some quality, for a quarter of the memory
choices.why: Right. The same weights are stored with fewer bits each, and rounding costs a little accuracy.

prompt: A 7B model at 8 bits needs 7 GB for its weights, and your machine has 8 GB free for it. You want it to read long documents. What does this lesson say to expect?
hint: The weights are the floor, not the total.

choices.text: No problem, since the weights fit with a gigabyte to spare
choices.why: The spare gigabyte has to hold the working memory for the context, which grows with its length.

choices.text: It runs, but answers in 8-bit text
choices.why: The width is about how weights are stored. The text it writes is the same kind of text.

choices.text: Trouble: working memory grows with the context, and almost none is left
choices.why: Right. The weights fit, but the text being processed needs memory too, and a long document needs more of it.

choices.text: It cannot run at all, as models only run at 16 bits
choices.why: Quantised models run; that is the point of quantising them.

prompt: You call a model through a provider's API. Whose problem is the memory its weights need?

choices.text: Yours, since the weights are downloaded to your machine with each request
choices.why: Nothing is downloaded. The request goes to the provider's machines and the reply comes back.

choices.text: Theirs, since they run the model for you; you pay per token
choices.why: Right. The arithmetic matters when you run the weights yourself.

choices.text: Yours: you choose the width in the request
choices.why: The width of a hosted model is the provider's choice, not a request setting.

choices.text: Nobody's, because API models do not have weights
choices.why: Every model has weights. With an API they sit on someone else's hardware.

prompt: Put the steps for working out whether a downloaded model fits your machine in order.
hint: Start from what the model card tells you.
items: Choose the width, and so the bytes per weight
Multiply them to get the memory for the weights
Leave room for the context and everything else running

prompt: Match each width to the bytes each weight takes.
A colleague says: "Our model learnt the new prices from yesterday's chats, since it saw them so many times." What does this lesson say?
hint: Did anything change the weights yesterday?

choices.text: That is right, since repetition is how training works
choices.why: Repetition matters in training. Chatting with a deployed model is not training it.

choices.text: It learnt them only if the chats used the same wording
choices.why: Wording does not matter here. Nothing in a chat changes the weights.

choices.text: It learnt them, but only until the provider resets it overnight
choices.why: There is nothing to reset. The weights never changed.

choices.text: The weights did not change; the chats were only input
choices.why: Right. Using a model does not train it. Lesson 9 is about changing the weights on purpose, and what that costs.
